title: Activation Probe Cost-Effectiveness Scaling: How Few Labels Do You Need?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: characterizing the label-efficiency curve for activation probes makes this defense technique accessible to more teams. If 50-100 labels suffice, it is trivially deployable. Practical engineering specification with clear safety impact.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires extracting activations from a model and training linear probes with sklearn. The pipeline is well-documented in referenced work. Intermediate ML knowledge needed for activation extraction, but probe training is standard.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment: vary label count, train probes, plot AUC curve. One model, one dataset (JailbreakBench), one clear deliverable (label-efficiency curve). Obvious output artifact that fits easily in 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: Activation probes for safety classification are established, but the specific question of label efficiency — plotting the AUC curve as a function of label count to determine the minimum viable labeled set — has not been directly studied in the safety domain. General work on probes (PING framework, HarmBench) mentions that probes require labeled data but does not characterize the label-efficiency curve. Active learning and few-shot approaches exist in adjacent domains but not applied to safety activation probes specifically. This is a practical engineering contribution with clear novelty.
